candidates.source_body_excerpt: Work is under way to create a new play area in Middleton and improve two others in the town. This week, Rochdale Council began work to create Mainway Meadows play area between Mainway and Moss Way in Alkrington. The new play area will include accessible pathways, safety fencing, inclusive play equipment, swings, a slide, seesaw, roundabout, seating, a children’s picnic table and more. Work is expected to take four to five weeks. Rochdale Council shared: “Thanks to Middleton Township funding, the play area will provide much-needed play facilities for local families, creating a safe, welcoming and inclusive space for children of different ages and abilities to enjoy.” Work is under way to create Mainway Meadows play area. Image: Rochdale Council Also in Alkrington, work to improve the play area at Sandy Park is almost complete. Cllr Dylan Williams shared: “It’s great to see the new play equipment we have invested in for Kirkway Stocks Play Park in Alkrington nearly finished (more commonly known as Farmway or Sandy Park).

candidates.source_title: Courteeners: From humble Manchester roots to the world - and back
candidates.source_summary: Courteeners frontman Liam Fray revisits the Manchester pub where he first got on stage in 2005.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Courteeners frontman Liam Fray revisits The Briton's Protection Pub in Manchester where he first performed more than 20 years ago The street outside legendary indie club 42s, a front garden on Burnage Lane and a pub's function room with a tiny stage - all locations in Manchester where you could have found Courteeners in their early days. The four school friends from Middleton, near Rochdale, have certainly come a long way since they hit the Manchester indie scene in 2006. While they have travelled around the world ever since, there is no place like home and they will take to the stage later for a huge homecoming gig at Wythenshawe Park. From humble beginnings performing for friends in the garden of their shared house in Burnage, the Courteeners are now celebrating 20 years together. Fresh from releasing a new best-of compilation album called God Bless The Band, lead singer and songwriter Liam Fray spoke to BBC North West Tonight at The Briton's Protection pub on Deansgate, where he first performed as a solo artist back in 2005. Courteeners performing at Glastonbury Festival in 2023 Sitting upstairs in the pub, Fray smiled at the 3ft (0.9m) stage and single spotlight on the ceiling while recalling the night he spent there more than two decades ago.

candidates.source_summary: The restoration of a unique set of historic steps which are more than 400 years old old has been completed in the heart of Rochdale town centre.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The restoration of a unique set of historic steps which are more than 400 years old old has been completed in the heart of Rochdale town centre. Running through the Broadfield Park Slopes, the Packer Spout steps link the major historic attractions of Rochdale Town Hall and its surrounding area to St Chad’s Church, the oldest church in the borough, parts of which have Saxon origins. Dating from sometime before 1660, the church steps have a rich history and were thought to be used by mourning relatives who would travel up the steps to St Chad’s Church, where they would scatter rue and rosemary in ‘God’s Acre’ (St Chad’s Churchyard) as an offering to ease the spirits of their loved ones. Situated in the recently restored Broadfield Park Slopes area, during the Victorian period, the steps ran directly through a notorious slum area, known as ‘the gank’. The gank was characterised by tightly packed housing, narrow passageways, high crime rates and large numbers of ‘houses of ill repute’. Many of the residents who worked in Rochdale’s mills would have lived out their lives in this area. The site is so steep that Oldham contractor Maysand, which delivered the work, had to devise a special pulley system with tracks and rollers to help transport the stone up the hill. The investigation was launched after 19 violent robberies were reported at Parklife Festival in Manchester in July this year. Victims reported being approached in crowded areas of the festival and asked to hand over valuable items, including mobile phones and jewellery. In several incidents, those who resisted, or who’s friends stepped in to help, were subjected to violence before their property was stolen. Investigators believe members of the group would walk through the crowds and pass stolen items back and forth making it difficult to track where the items had gone. Officers responded immediately to reports of the offences and carried out extensive CCTV enquiries during the festival, which led to the identification of a suspect by the victims. candidates.source_title: Rochdale Youth Council leader Daniel Murphy announces immediate resignation
candidates.source_summary: Daniel Murphy has announced his resignation from his roles with Rochdale Youth Council and Youth Council UK with immediate effect.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Mr Murphy said he had made the decision after “careful reflection” and that he would continue to support young people outside his formal roles.

Mr Murphy described himself in his resignation announcement as leader of Rochdale Youth Council and Youth Cabinet and an elected board member of the Youth Council UK Executive Board.

He said: “Serving these positions has been an immense privilege. Being nominated by Rochdale Youth Service and democratically elected by peers to help set priorities, lead campaigns, and represent more than 7.8 million young people has been one of the greatest honours of my life so far.

“I remain passionate about ensuring every young person’s voice is heard, valued, and represented regardless of background.”

Mr Murphy did not give a specific reason for his resignation but said there “have to be boundaries”.

He said: “I want the focus to remain firmly on the priorities that matter to young people — safeguarding, mental health, equality of opportunity, violence against young women and girls, digital pressures, and genuine influence on decision-makers — rather than on any individual.”

He thanked Rochdale Youth Service, fellow Youth Cabinet members, the Youth Council UK Executive Board and member organisations, as well as local supporters, family and friends.

Mr Murphy added: “I will support a smooth transition in any way I can and will continue to champion young people from outside these formal roles.”

He later reiterated in his statement: “I am resigning from my roles with immediate effect after careful reflection.

“I am grateful for the opportunity to represent and advocate for young people.

“However, I believe there have to be boundaries, and stepping down is the right decision for me.”

candidates.source_title: Wardle man lends his voice to poetry trail about recovery
candidates.source_summary: A Wardle man who has been in recovery from substance use for just over a year has contributed to a new poetry and audio walking trail.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
A Wardle man who has been in recovery from substance use for just over a year has contributed to a new poetry and audio walking trail.

John Bailey is one of 15 people from Turning Point's Rochdale and Oldham Active Recovery service, known as ROAR, who worked with poet Phil Davenport on the project.

The group created seven spoken poetry pieces for If You Could Speak to the World, a self-guided walking route from Oldham town centre into Northern Roots.

Their recordings have been combined with music composed by Sophie Cooper and performed by Milnrow Band.

Mr Bailey, a former bar and restaurant manager, took part in outdoor sessions at Northern Roots during the spring and early summer.

The participants, aged from their 20s to their 70s, used the landscape to help create poetry and record sounds for the trail.

They also helped map the route and identify stopping points.

Mr Bailey said: “A big part of my recovery has been saying yes to things. And as an English literature graduate who grew up going on lots of walks, this opportunity really stood out for me.”

He is currently undertaking peer mentor training with ROAR ahead of postgraduate study in counselling and psychotherapy.

Describing one of the techniques used during the project, he said: “Phil had us write down answers to three questions: who we were grateful to and what message we would send them, what we look back on with sadness and what we thought the area we were walking through was like 150 years ago.

“We then 'curated' our own words to make a 'found poem' out of them. They were surprisingly profound and beautiful and, in this way, everyone in the group created a piece they could feel proud of.”

The shortest version of the trail is two miles and takes in all seven locations, while longer routes run for up to six miles.

Maps will be available from the Northern Roots Welcome Building and online from September.

Davenport said: “This is a sound walk like no other. We aren’t delivering a nature trail or a local history, but something much more unusual. We will be guided by the voices of local people in recovery: people who are intensely aware of the dark art of damage and the honesty needed to pull away from it.

“Their poems are the narrative for the walk, which takes us out of a busy, chaotic town centre, to the edge of where people are and then out beyond, into the woods and the wilds.”

The project was commissioned by visual arts organisation Portraits of Recovery for Recoverist Month and funded through Transport for Greater Manchester's Wheels and Walks programme.

Guided walks are due to take place during September and October to launch the permanent audio trail.

“So, come on, sharpen those coloured pencils and felt tips — or use whatever materials you like — and show us your best Christmas design inspired by Christmas on the ELR. We can’t wait to see what our young artists come up with!”

Entries should be emailed to submissions@eastlancsrailway.co.uk by 9am on 25 September.

The railway said the winner would be announced shortly after the deadline.

East Lancashire Railway operates from Bolton Street Station in Bury along a 12.5-mile route between Heywood and Rawtenstall.

candidates.source_title: Police appeal for witnesses following death of man in Bury
candidates.source_summary: Police are appealing for information following the death of a man who was reportedly assaulted in Bury town centre.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Greater Manchester Police said the man became unwell outside the Sky Bar at around 8.45pm on Wednesday 22 July after reportedly being assaulted.

He was taken to hospital in a critical condition and died on Saturday 15 August.

His family are being supported by specialist officers.

A man who was arrested on suspicion of assault has since been charged.

Police are now seeking to speak to a man pictured as part of their appeal, who they believe was seen with the victim outside the Sky Bar at around 7.30pm on 22 July.

Officers also want to hear from anyone who was in or around the venue that evening and may have information about what happened.

Senior investigating officer Duncan Thorpe said: “While a man has been charged in connection with this case, our enquiries remain ongoing and we are continuing to piece together the events of that evening.

“We are particularly keen to speak to anyone who was at or around the Sky Bar in Bury town centre on Wednesday 22 July and may have seen this incident or has information about what happened.

candidates.source_title: Drug dealer jailed after being shot by police during Whitefield arrest
candidates.source_summary: A drug dealer who was shot in the arm by police as officers attempted to arrest him in Whitefield has been jailed for six years and 10 months.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Lewis Hanson was sentenced at Manchester Crown Court today, Thursday 27 August, after admitting drug and firearms offences.

Hanson, 20, of no fixed address, pleaded guilty to possession with intent to supply Class A and B drugs, possession of a prohibited firearm, conspiracy to supply a firearm, possession of ammunition and being concerned in the supply of controlled drugs.

Greater Manchester Police's Serious and Organised Crime Group had been monitoring Hanson's movements on Friday 22 May.

Police said he was seen driving a white Cupra Ateca around Radcliffe, Whitefield and Greenmount and repeatedly returning to an address in Chapelfield.

Officers also saw Hanson meeting a number of people in what police believed was activity consistent with suspected drug supply.

At around 3pm, officers attempted to stop the Cupra on Bury New Road in Whitefield.

GMP said Hanson attempted to evade arrest and an officer discharged a single shot, striking him in the arm.

He was detained and taken to hospital. Police said his injury was not life-threatening or life-changing.

Officers subsequently searched the address in Chapelfield and recovered a converted Retay Model 17 blank-firing pistol, which is prohibited under the Firearms Act.

Ammunition was found concealed in a black bin bag inside a bedroom wardrobe.

Police also seized Class A and B drugs, scales, vacuum-packed bags and empty snap bags.

Detective Superintendent Joe Harrop, of GMP's Serious Crime Division, said: “Hanson played a key role in the supply of illegal drugs throughout Bury and beyond, our investigation uncovered evidence of drug dealing and with the recovery of a prohibited firearm at an address linked to him.

“Ammunition and drug supply paraphernalia were also found, underlining the lengths he may have gone to, to protect his interests.

“The presence of a converted firearm in these circumstances is deeply concerning and demonstrates the dangerous environment often associated with organised criminal activity.

“Drug dealing and firearms have a devastating impact on our communities. They fuel exploitation, violence and fear, and we know that residents want this type of criminality removed from their area, and we are doing all we can to do exactly that.

“We will continue to relentlessly pursue those involved in the supply of drugs, the possession of illegal firearms and organised criminality. We remain committed to protecting our communities, disrupting criminal networks and bringing offenders to justice.”

candidates.source_title: Simister Island overnight closures planned
candidates.source_summary: Simister Island on the M60 will be closed overnight this week and next week as part of the major works on the junction.
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Tonight (August 26), from 9pm until 6am, junction 18 will be shut. The same overnight closures will also take place tomorrow (August 27), September 1 and September 2.

National Highways made the decision to avoid these closures over the bank holiday weekend, according to their website. Diversion routes will be put in place for those passing through.

These works form part of the major interchange upgrade, currently estimated to be completed by 2030. The project will see five lanes of traffic and a new link road will be created at Junction 18 in a bid to ease congestion, following official confirmation by the Department for Transport (DfT) last year.

Simister Island interchange, which connects the M60, M62 and M66 motorways, is notorious for being one of the North West’s busiest motorway junctions. The scheme – estimated to cost between £255m and £296m – aims to reduce congestion, improve journey times and create a safer route.

The junction is used by around 90,000 vehicles each day, according to National Highways.

The project itself will see a ‘northern loop’ built to stop thousands of vehicles using the current traffic light controlled roundabout every day. A five-lane section on both sides of the M60 between Prestwich and Simister (junctions 17 and 18) has been touted as well.

The M66 on the Bury side of the junction would also be widened with new lanes introduced at the interchange and a second lane added from the M60 northbound link.

National Highways said: “Simister Island Interchange is one of the busiest motorway junctions in the north-west used by around 90,000 vehicles each day. The junction struggles with such high volumes of traffic above what it was designed for, and as a result suffers from congestion and poor journey time reliability.

“The project will improve junction 18 of the M60 and facilitate smoother flows of traffic along the connecting motorways, contributing to more reliable and safer journeys into and around Greater Manchester.”

candidates.source_title: Energy Secretary responds to Ofgem's £60 a year energy price cap increase
candidates.source_summary: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has made a statement regarding Ofgem's announcement of the next energy price cap which is to take effect in October of this year, costing the average household £60 a year
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
Fahnbulleh said: 'Families will be understandably concerned about the cost of energy bills this winter, which is being driven up by the Iran War.  

'Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.  

'This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.'

The price cap announced by Ofgem is a rise of 4%, a three-year high, costing the average household around £5 a month, equating to £60 a year. This comes after Andy Burnham announced the removal of VAT from electricity bills, and the speculation around whether Burnham will begin drilling in the North Sea.

The Iran War began on 28 February 2026, with US-Israeli strikes killing numerous senior Iranian officials, including the Iranian Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. This instigated the still ongoing war between allies America and Israel against Iran, that has led to the Strait of Hormuz, a key area regarding the movement of oil, located at the southern border of Iran, undergoing immense disruption, drastically decreasing the amount of maritime traffic in the area.

The Strait of Hormuz, prior to the war, carried roughly 20% of the world's petroleum consumption according to Times Now, with around 130 ships making journeys through the Strait of Hormuz daily. Due to the disruptions, including the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, oil and energy prices have risen across the globe, with the pre-war baseline for Brent crude oil being around $72 a barrel, which jumped to almost $120 at its peak. Today, the price of a barrel of Brent crude is $86.27. This has declined from the $100 spike just over a month ago for a barrel of Brent crude.

The reverberations of the catastrophic consequences of the Iran War have been felt on energy bills across the country, with the BBC reporting that the 'typical' bill will rise to £1862, which would be a rise of £221 a year.

However, Fahnbulleh was asked on LBC if the rise in bills was solely due to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and in Ukraine, or if government policy regarding renewable subsidies also has been contributing to the rise in energy bills. The Energy Secretary responded saying that 'it is both'. She later said that 'for the grid to operate properly, we've got to upgrade it', blaming the previous government for a lack of investment in the energy grid over their 14 years in power. Ofgem have said that household energy bills would have been £45 higher per year if Andy Burnham had not removed VAT from electricity bills.

A record number of candidates received results across the country: a total of 70,411 students, up 15 per cent on 2024. “The results this year have been very good, with many students achieving top grades across a wide range of subjects,” said Eamon, adding: “These achievements will open doors to further education and career opportunities and we are confident that our students will continue to excel in whatever paths they choose to pursue. “To witness our students return this morning with great excitement about the future ahead is one of the best days of the school year. We are very proud of each student. Their success is a testament not only to their individual efforts but also to the support and encouragement provided by our dedicated teaching staff, supportive parents and the wider Heywood community. “Our teachers and SNAs have gone above and beyond to provide a learning environment that nurtures each student's potential, even in the face of challenges which have unfolded during their time here. “On a personal level, I took great satisfaction chatting to many of the students this morning who visited the school and heard of the plans they have made for their future. Many have already secured employment or are accessing apprenticeships with local employers.” Eamon noted that with the changing employment landscape and “demand in certain sectors,” students are being very strategic in their career choice and “not merely following the media-driven route of third-level without assessing if it best suits their talents,” he said.

candidates.source_title: Historic mill to be turned into apartments - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_summary: The second part of an historic mill in Rochdale will be turned into apartments.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The second part of an historic mill in Rochdale will be turned into apartments. Home Grace Co Ltd has been granted permission by Rochdale Council to turn commercial units on the ground floor of Sudden Mill in Manchester Road into three apartments. It follows planning permission granted to turn the first floor into five apartments. The mill was previously occupied by the Homegrace Outlet, which sold pillows and bedding. The site is next to Sudden Brook and close to the roundabout with Manchester Road, Bolton Road and Silk Road. Sudden Mill is included on the council’s register of non-designated heritage assets which does not allow for any external changes to be made without planning permission. The earliest Ordnance Survey maps of the area show the site as open space in the 1840s, likely to have been agricultural land. By the 1890s, the site was occupied by the Littlefields Cotton Mill. It had 320 looms, manufacturing T-cloths, flanelettes and other material.
